coach_says: Before pushing d4, count who attacks that square: Black's e5 pawn, the c6 knight and the b6 bishop hit d4 three times, and you defend it only twice (Nf3 and the queen). So after 8...Nxd4 you simply lose a pawn, and Nxe2+ also takes your good bishop. The quiet d3 keeps everything protected; if you want d4 later, prepare it first (for example with Na4 to swap off the b6 bishop, or c3).

The d4 pawn was free: 13...Bxd4 wins it, because if White recaptures with exd4 the e-file opens and Rxe1+ Qxe1 Qxd4+ forks the king and the c4 bishop. The e3 pawn was really a shield for the e1 rook, so it could not take back safely. When an opponent's pawn looks defended, check whether the defender is also guarding something else.
concept: pawn defender tied to the rook

coach_says: Castling put your king on g1, where the d4 knight jumps to e2 with check and forks the king and the queen on g3: Ne2+ wins your queen. Before you move, look at every check your opponent has; the knight on d4 was already eyeing c2 and e2. Nc3 kept you a piece up by covering e2 and e4.
also: check every enemy check before moving

coach_says: Your e6 knight was the only piece guarding g7, which the queen on f7 and the bishop on d4 were both aiming at. Taking the pawn on g5 pulled it away and Bxg7 is checkmate. Before you move a piece, ask what it is defending; here you had to keep g7 covered or trade off the d4 bishop with Nxd4.

After 11.d4 the e4 pawn had no defender, so 11...Nxe4 simply wins it. Taking on d4 instead let White push e4-e5, hitting your bishop and knight at the same time; you can hold with Re8, pinning the pawn, but the free pawn was gone. When your opponent strikes in the centre, look first for anything they left loose.

You are a pawn down, and Qxa5 swaps queens and then wins the d7 pawn back with Rxd7, reaching a rook ending that is close to a draw. Qxd7 also wins a pawn but keeps queens on after Re1+ and Rxd1: a queen ending a pawn down, with Black's passed b-pawn and your exposed king facing checks, is very hard to hold. When you are behind, trade the pieces that make your opponent's extra pawn dangerous.

Retreating to h3 puts the knight on the rim and does nothing about Black's main idea, ...Nd4, which hits your queen on f3 and the c2 pawn (Nxc2+ forks king and rook). After Nh3 Nd4 your queen has only g3 to go to. The move c3 takes d4 away from the knight and prepares d4 yourself; when the opponent has a strong jump into your camp, take that square away first.

Your e4 pawn was attacked by the f6 knight and nothing defended it, so after cxd4 Black just takes it with Nxe4. Pushing 12.e5 saves the pawn with a threat, hitting the d6 bishop and the f6 knight at once; Black has to answer with Re8 and you then recapture on d4. When a pawn is attacked, see if it can step forward and attack something.
concept: hanging pawn: push it with tempo

coach_says: The e3 pawn was attacked twice (your rook on e8 and queen on g5) and defended only once by the e2 rook, so 16...Rxe3 wins it: Rxe3 Qxe3+ and you keep the extra pawn. It also takes your rook off e8, so White's threat of Bxf7+ no longer hits it. Re7 parried the threat but left the pawn; look for a capture that solves your problem and wins material at the same time.

Your king is still in the centre, and f5 opens the diagonal from h5 to e8: Qh5+ follows and you can no longer castle, so your king gets chased while White opens the e-file and c-file. Instead, finish development and get the king safe with Qc8 or Nbc6 and then castle. With the king uncastled, be very careful about moving the f-pawn.

Your a2 pawn was hanging to the rook on a8, so grabbing b6 just trades it for a2, and Black's rook lands on your second rank where it attacks b2 and c2 while your queen is off on b6. First secure the loose pawn with a3, then think about winning b6, which is not going anywhere. Before taking a pawn, check what your opponent takes back.

Ra5 is a reasonable move: it brings the loose rook back towards the centre and keeps the d-pawn defended. You are worse because White's queen and bishop are so active, but this move is about as good as the alternatives. Keep looking for ways to trade your opponent's strongest piece.
Ne5 is a good move: the knight jumps into a strong central square, eyes f7 and c6, and you keep a clear advantage. d5 was slightly stronger, kicking the bishop first, but both are fine.
2.Bc4, the Bishop's Opening, is a perfectly good choice: it develops a piece and aims at f7. Nf3 is more common, but this is a matter of taste.

The position was already very hard, but notice your c5 bishop was attacked by the e5 rook and undefended. Kd6 guards it with the king, but then Rd5+ (protected by the c4 pawn) gives check and next Rxc5 wins the bishop anyway. Moving the bishop to safety, for example Be7, was better; defending with the king often walks it into checks.

Qb3 is fine: your c2 pawn was attacked by the c8 rook, and the queen now defends it while also pressing on d5. It is as good as anything here. You are a pawn down, so keep your pieces active and your c-pawn defended.
1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is a solid, respected reply to 1.e4. It prepares d5 to challenge the centre. Nothing wrong here.

You are up material, but your king has no escape square: Black plays Bh2+, and after Kh1 the bishop moves again with a discovered check from the h8 rook, then back to h2, giving a perpetual check and a draw. a5 ignored that threat. Ra1 (or Rd1) frees f1 for the king so Bh2+ is met by Kf1. When you are winning, first make your king safe from checks, then push your pawns.
also: give your king an escape square

coach_says: Qg7+ walks your queen onto the g-file, where Rg2 pins it to your king and it is attacked twice (rook and queen) and defended only by the king, so you lose the queen for a rook. Instead 29...Qxe5 just takes the free e5 pawn with your queen backed by the e8 rook, and your queen is centralised and safe. Before giving a check, ask what the opponent can block with, and whether the block attacks you.

Taking the knight with bxa5 removed the b4 pawn, which was the only thing blocking Black's queen on d6 from your knight on a3. Black replies Qxa3 and the a5 pawn soon falls too, so you end up worse off than before. Nxb5 first moves the knight to safety with an attack on the queen. Before recapturing, check which lines your capturing pawn was blocking.
concept: recapture opened a line to the knight
